title: Refactoring
locators: CC24 (Code Complete 2nd ed. ch. 24 'Refactoring': kinds of software evolution, reasons to refactor, specific refactorings, refactoring safely, refactoring strategies); PP 'Refactoring' (The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th anniversary ed., ch. 7 'While You Are Coding', topic 'Refactoring'); the 97 Things essay 'Before You Refactor' (97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know en/thing_06/README.md)
candidate_evidence: Kim, Zimmermann, Nagappan, 'A field study of refactoring challenges and benefits' (FSE 2012; IEEE TSE 2014 extension) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'the refactoring definition in practice is not confined to a rigorous definition of semantics-preserving code transformations and that developers perceive that refactoring involves substantial cost and risks'; 'binary modules refactored by this team experienced significant reduction in the number of inter-module dependencies and post-release defects' — https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/?p=163533; slides at web.cs.ucla.edu/~miryung/Publications/fse2012-refactoringstudy-slides.pdf

Murphy-Hill, Parnin, Black, 'How we refactor, and how we know it' (ICSE 2009; IEEE TSE 2012) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'four data sets spanning more than 13,000 developers, 240,000 tool-assisted refactorings, 2,500 developer hours, and 3,400 version control commits'; 'cast doubt on several previously stated assumptions about how programmers refactor, while validating others' — https://people.scs.carleton.ca/~jeanpier/Fall2021/Topic%204-%20About%20Smells%20and%20Refactoring/5-%20HowWeRefactor-icse09.pdf (course copy)

Silva, Tsantalis, Valente, 'Why we refactor? Confessions of GitHub contributors' (FSE 2016; arXiv:1607.02459) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'a catalogue of 44 distinct motivations for 12 well-known refactoring types'; 'refactoring activity is mainly driven by changes in requirements and much less by code smells'; 'Extract Method was found to be the most versatile refactoring operation serving 11 different purposes' — https://arxiv.org/pdf/1607.02459

Bavota, De Carluccio, De Lucia, Di Penta, Oliveto, Strollo, 'When does a refactoring induce bugs? An empirical study' (SCAM 2012, best paper) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'three Java software systems (Apache Ant, Xerces, and ArgoUML)'; '15,008 refactoring operations (of 52 different kinds) using the Ref-Finder tool'; 'the SZZ algorithm to determine whether refactorings induced faults'; 'While some kinds of refactorings are unlikely to be harmful, others, such as refactorings involving hierarchies (e.g., pull up method), tend to induce faults very frequently' — https://people.lu.usi.ch/bavotg/papers/scam2012.pdf (author copy)

Di Penta, Bavota, Zampetti, 'On the relationship between refactoring actions and bugs: a differentiated replication' (ESEC/FSE 2020; arXiv:2009.11685) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'answers the same research questions on a much larger dataset (3 vs 103 systems)'; 'The results of the quantitative analysis confirm the findings of the replicated study, while the qualitative analysis partially demystifies the role played by refactoring actions in the bug introduction' — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2009.11685

Tsantalis, Mansouri, Eshkevari, Mazinanian, Dig, 'Accurate and efficient refactoring detection in commit history' (ICSE 2018) — RefactoringMiner; its catalog of detected refactoring types is in tsantalis/RefactoringMiner master README.md

Golubev, Kurbatova, AlOmar, Bryksin, Mkaouer, 'One thousand and one stories: a large-scale survey of software refactoring' (ESEC/FSE 2021 industry, pp. 1303–1313; arXiv:2107.07357) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'a survey targeting 1,183 users of IntelliJ-based IDEs'; 'almost two-thirds of developers spend more than one hour in a single session refactoring their code; that refactoring types vary greatly in popularity; and that a lot of developers would like to know more about IDE refactoring features but lack the means to do so' — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2107.07357; a neverworkintheory.org review exists (2022/03/04/software-refactoring.html)

Mens, Tourwé, 'A survey of software refactoring' (IEEE TSE 30(2), 2004; DOI 10.1109/TSE.2004.1265817) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'an extensive overview of existing research in the field of software refactoring ... the refactoring activities supported, techniques and formalisms used, types of software artifacts being refactored, important issues for building refactoring tool support, and the effect of refactoring on the software process' — https://sites.cc.gatech.edu/morale/tools/isvis/2009/summaries/A_Survey_of_Software_Refactoring.pdf (course copy)

official and tool documentation: google/eng-practices master review/developer/small-cls.md §'Separate Out Refactorings'; golang/tools master gopls/doc/features/transformation.md (Rename, refactor.extract, refactor.inline.call, refactor.inline.variable as tool-performed behaviour-preserving transformations); the refactoring catalog on refactoring.com and IDE refactoring documentation on vendor sites are not openable
notes: Owns the behaviour-preserving transformation and its safety: refactoring only under tests that pass before and after, one transformation at a time with the tests run between steps, tool-performed transformations over hand edits where a tool exists, extra care with hierarchy-changing refactorings that the evidence ties to induced faults, and refactoring as preparation for the change at hand rather than as a free-standing rewrite. Yields the diagnosis of what to refactor to code-smells-and-antipatterns; getting untested code under a safety net to seams-and-characterization-tests; repository-wide automated rewrites to large-scale-changes-and-migrations; keeping structural and behavioural edits in separate commits (the size and shape of one change) to small-steps-and-minimal-diffs; duplicated code blocks to duplication-and-single-source-of-truth; routine length and parameter count to routine-size-and-parameters; renaming a public API that external callers use to api-evolution-and-deprecation. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that depends on one IDE's or one language's refactoring tool belongs elsewhere, and a tool name may appear in an Example only.

title: Code smells and antipatterns
locators: CC24 (Code Complete 2nd ed. ch. 24 'Refactoring', the 'Reasons to Refactor' list of warning signs); the smell catalog the topic is usually formulated from is Fowler and Beck, Refactoring 2nd ed. ch. 3 'Bad Smells in Code' — a trade book, named as formulation only
candidate_evidence: Tufano, Palomba, Bavota, Oliveto, Di Penta, De Lucia, Poshyvanyk, 'When and why your code starts to smell bad' (ICSE 2015, distinguished paper; IEEE TSE 2017 extension) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'over 579,000 software changes in 200 projects'; 'symptoms of problems frequently evident from the inception of pieces of code rather than creeping in gradually through incremental changes' — https://people.lu.usi.ch/bavotg/papers/icse2015_badSmells.pdf (author copy)

Sjøberg, Yamashita, Anda, Mockus, Dybå, 'Quantifying the effect of code smells on maintenance effort' (IEEE TSE 39(8), 2013, pp. 1144–1156) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'Six developers were hired to perform three maintenance tasks each on four functionally equivalent Java systems'; 'None of the 12 investigated smells was significantly associated with increased effort after adjusting for file size and the number of changes; Refused Bequest was significantly associated with decreased effort. File size and the number of changes explained almost all of the modeled variation in effort'; 'a focus on reducing code size and the work practices that limit the number of changes may be more beneficial than refactoring code smells' — https://web-backend.simula.no/sites/default/files/publications/Simula.simula.1460.pdf (author copy)

Palomba, Bavota, Di Penta, Fasano, Oliveto, De Lucia, 'On the diffuseness and the impact on maintainability of code smells: a large scale empirical investigation' (Empirical Software Engineering 23, 2018) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: '395 releases of 30 open source projects and considering 17,350 manually validated instances of 13 different code smell kinds'; 'smells characterized by long and/or complex code (e.g., Complex Class) are highly diffused, and that smelly classes have a higher change- and fault-proneness than smell-free classes' — https://www.iris.unisa.it/bitstream/11386/4708436/2/J9.pdf (author copy)

Khomh, Di Penta, Guéhéneuc, Antoniol, 'An exploratory study of the impact of antipatterns on class change- and fault-proneness' (Empirical Software Engineering 17(3), 2012) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: '13 antipatterns in 54 releases of ArgoUML, Eclipse, Mylyn, and Rhino'; 'whether these odds are due to class sizes or antipatterns'; 'In almost all releases of the four systems, classes participating in antipatterns are more change- and fault-prone than others' — https://publications.polymtl.ca/2642/
Silva, Tsantalis, Valente, 'Why we refactor? Confessions of GitHub contributors' (FSE 2016) — refactoring is driven mainly by requirement changes, much less by smells

tool rules on class-level smells: PMD design category (pmd/pmd main pmd-java/src/main/resources/category/java/design.xml: GodClass, DataClass, TooManyMethods, CouplingBetweenObjects, ExcessiveImports, SwitchDensity), Checkstyle metrics checks (checkstyle/checkstyle master src/site/xdoc/checks/metrics/classfanoutcomplexity.xml, classdataabstractioncoupling.xml), Pylint design checker (pylint-dev/pylint main pylint/checkers/design_analysis.py: too-many-instance-attributes, too-many-public-methods, too-few-public-methods, too-many-ancestors), ESLint max-classes-per-file (eslint/eslint main docs/src/rules/max-classes-per-file.md)

tool rules on dead code: ESLint no-unused-vars and no-unreachable (docs/src/rules/no-unused-vars.md, no-unreachable.md), PMD bestpractices UnusedPrivateMethod, UnusedPrivateField, UnusedLocalVariable, UnusedFormalParameter (category/java/bestpractices.xml), Ruff F841 unused-variable (crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/pyflakes/rules/unused_variable.rs), go vet unreachable (golang/tools master go/analysis/passes/unreachable/doc.go)
the smell catalog pages on refactoring.com and martinfowler.com are not openable; the book is formulation only
notes: Owns the smells with no owner of their own: large or god class, data class, feature envy, divergent change and shotgun surgery, speculative generality, lazy class, temporary field, dead code and commented-out code; it names the smell as a reason to look, and the fix travels through refactoring. Yields duplicated code blocks to duplication-and-single-source-of-truth; routine length and parameter count to routine-size-and-parameters; message chains and dependency direction to coupling-and-dependency-direction; pass-through methods and shallow modules to complexity-and-deep-modules; refused bequest and deep hierarchies to inheritance-versus-composition; primitive obsession to domain-modeling-and-domain-language; the transformation itself to refactoring; a smell left deliberately and recorded to technical-debt. The evidence is mixed once size is controlled (Sjøberg 2013 against Khomh 2012 and Palomba 2018), so a card states each smell's effect with the source's own precondition and never as an absolute. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a class-level smell carries applies_to object-oriented where it presupposes classes, and a smell that exists in one language only belongs elsewhere.

title: Seams and characterization tests
locators: WELC (Working Effectively with Legacy Code, Feathers 2004: ch. 4 'The Seam Model'; ch. 6 'I Don't Have Much Time and I Have to Change It' — sprout method and class, wrap method and class; ch. 13 'I Need to Make a Change, but I Don't Know What Tests to Write' — characterization tests; Part III 'Dependency-Breaking Techniques', ch. 25); SEG13 (Software Engineering at Google ch. 13 'Test Doubles', where it treats seams)
candidate_evidence: Fraser, Arcuri, 'EvoSuite: automatic test suite generation for object-oriented software' (ESEC/FSE 2011) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'EvoSuite suggests possible oracles by adding small and effective sets of assertions that concisely summarize the current behavior'; 'optimizes whole test suites towards satisfying a coverage criterion' — https://www.st.cs.uni-saarland.de/publications/details/fraser-fse-2011

Xie, 'Augmenting automatically generated unit-test suites with regression oracle checking' (ECOOP 2006, pp. 380–403; DOI 10.1007/11785477_23) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'Orstra first executes the test suite and collects the class under test's object states, then creates assertions for asserting behavior of the object states, and also creates assertions for executed observer methods (public methods with non-void returns) to assert their return values'; 'an automatically generated test suite's fault-detection capability can be effectively improved after being augmented by Orstra' — https://dblp.dagstuhl.de/rec/conf/ecoop/Xie06.html

Pacheco, Lahiri, Ernst, Ball, 'Feedback-directed random test generation' (ICSE 2007; ICSE most influential paper 2017) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'As soon as an input is built, it is executed and checked against a set of contracts and filters. The result of the execution determines whether the input is redundant, illegal, contract-violating, or useful for generating more inputs'; 'On 14 large, widely-used libraries (comprising 780KLOC), feedback-directed random test generation finds many previously-unknown errors'; the tool is Randoop — https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~mernst/pubs/feedback-testgen-icse2007-abstract.html (author abstract page)

Shamshiri, Just, Rojas, Fraser, McMinn, Arcuri, 'Do automatically generated unit tests find real faults? An empirical study of effectiveness and challenges' (ASE 2015, pp. 201–211, distinguished paper) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'three state-of-the-art unit test generation tools for Java (Randoop, EvoSuite, and Agitar) to the 357 real faults in the Defects4J dataset'; 'Although the automatically generated test suites detected 55.7% of the faults overall, only 19.9% of all the individual test suites detected a fault'; improvement areas '2) improving the propagation of faulty program states to an observable output, coupled with the generation of more sensitive assertions, and 3) improving the simulation of the execution environment to detect faults that are dependent on external factors such as date and time' — https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~rjust/publ/unit_test_generation_effectiveness_ase_2015.pdf (author copy)

Zaidman, Van Rompaey, van Deursen, Demeyer, 'Studying the co-evolution of production and test code in open source and industrial developer test processes through repository mining' (Empirical Software Engineering 16, 2011, pp. 325–364) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'investigates how test code and production code should co-evolve within software development processes, proposing three views (realized by a tool called TeMo) that combine information from a software project's versioning system, artifact sizes, and test coverage reports' — https://win.uantwerpen.be/~sdemey/Pubs/summ/ZaidmanEMSE2011.html; TU Delft repository copies listed in the result

'Snapshot testing in practice: benefits and drawbacks' (JSS 2023) — the orchestrator's search did not surface the article itself; a related 2024 master's thesis (homepages.dcc.ufmg.br/~mtov/diss/2024-victor.pdf) and 'LLMShot: reducing snapshot testing maintenance via LLMs' (arXiv:2507.10062) are the results; the snippet relayed: 'Snapshot testing is adopted due to its ease of implementation, allowing developers to write more tests and consequently prevent regressions' and 'When failures occur, developers must triage each failure to determine whether it represents a regression or reflects intentional changes' — treat the JSS article as unconfirmed by this search

official documentation of snapshot and golden-file tests: jestjs/jest main docs/SnapshotTesting.md; mitsuhiko/insta master README.md (Rust); golang/go master src/cmd/go/alldocs.go (the go tool ignores a directory named 'testdata', the home of golden files)

official documentation of seams per language: golang/website master _content/doc/effective_go.html 'Interfaces and other types'; python/cpython main Doc/library/unittest.mock.rst §'Where to patch' (a patch target is a seam); rust-lang/book main src/ch10-02-traits.md on trait bounds as the parameter seam
SEG13 on abseil.io is not openable; the seam model and the dependency-breaking catalog are a trade book, formulation only
notes: Owns putting untested code under a safety net before changing it: finding a seam where behaviour can be substituted without editing the code under test (an object or interface seam, a parameter seam, a module or link seam), the smallest dependency-breaking edit that makes a unit constructible in a test (parameterize a constructor, extract an interface, sprout or wrap new behaviour instead of editing inside it), and characterization tests that pin the observed behaviour, snapshot and golden-file tests included, with the rule that a pinned oddity is recorded, not silently fixed in the same change. Yields the choice among fakes, stubs and mocks and speccing a double to test-doubles; assertion quality and test structure to unit-testing-and-test-quality; end-to-end golden tests to larger-tests-integration-and-end-to-end; test-first development of new code to test-first-and-test-driven-development; the refactoring done once the net is in place to refactoring. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; the preprocessing seam exists in C and C++ only and is out of scope, and a seam that one language's runtime alone offers (monkey-patching a module) is named as that language's form of a general seam, never as the rule.

title: Large-scale changes and migrations
locators: SEG22 (Software Engineering at Google ch. 22 'Large-Scale Changes': what a large-scale change is, why atomic changes are hard, the infrastructure and the process); SW3.8 (SWEBOK Guide V4.0 ch. 4 'Software Construction' §3.8)
candidate_evidence: Wright, Jasper, Klimek, Carruth, Wan, 'Large-scale automated refactoring using ClangMR' (ICSM 2013, pp. 548–551) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'combining the Clang compiler framework and the MapReduce parallel processor called ClangMR to enable code maintainers to easily and correctly transform large collections of code'; 'experiences using it in a recent API update with Google's C++ codebase' — https://research.google/pubs/pub41342/

Potvin, Levenberg, 'Why Google stores billions of lines of code in a single repository' (CACM 59(7), 2016) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'approximately one billion files with a history of approximately 35 million commits'; advantages 'unified versioning, extensive code sharing and reuse, simplified dependency management, atomic changes, large-scale refactoring, and collaboration across teams'; trade-offs 'tooling investments, codebase complexity with unnecessary dependencies, and effort invested in code health' — https://research.google/pubs/pub45424/

Ramanathan, Clapp, Barik, Sridharan, 'Piranha: reducing feature flag debt at Uber' (ICSE SEIP 2020) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'Piranha takes as input the name of the flag, expected treatment behavior, and the name of the flag's author, and it analyzes the ASTs of the program to generate appropriate refactorings which are packaged into a diff'; 'At Uber, Piranha has been used to remove around two thousand stale feature flags and their related code' — https://2020.icse-conferences.org/details/icse-2020-Software-Engineering-in-Practice/16/Piranha-Reducing-Feature-Flag-Debt-at-Uber; https://www.uber.com/blog/piranha/; the tool and its README at uber/piranha (GitHub, openable)

Dig, Johnson, 'How do APIs evolve? A story of refactoring' (Journal of Software Maintenance and Evolution 18(2), 2006, pp. 83–107) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'studied the API changes of four frameworks and one library, discovering that the breaking changes are not random but tend to fall into particular categories, with over 80% of these changes being refactorings' — https://ideals.illinois.edu/items/11029/bitstreams/40643/data.pdf (institutional copy)

Kim, Cai, Kim, 'An empirical investigation into the role of API-level refactorings during software evolution' (ICSE 2011) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'three large open source projects, totaling 26,523 revisions of evolution'; 'there is an increase in the number of bug fixes after API-level refactorings, and the time taken to fix bugs is shorter after API-level refactorings than before'; 'API-level refactorings occur more frequently before than after major software releases' — https://web.cs.ucla.edu/~miryung/Publications/icse11-refactoringbug.pdf (author copy)

Ivers, Nord, Ozkaya, Seifried, Timperley, Kessentini, 'Industry experiences with large-scale refactoring' (ESEC/FSE 2022; arXiv:2202.00173) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'results from 107 industry developers demonstrating that projects commonly undergo multiple large-scale refactorings, each requiring considerable effort'; 'while there is often a desire to refactor, other business concerns such as developing new features often take higher priority' — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2202.00173

official and tool documentation of automated migration: openrewrite/rewrite main README.md (recipes); golang/tools master gopls/doc/features/transformation.md §'refactor.inline.call'; rust-lang/edition-guide master src/editions/transitioning-an-existing-project-to-a-new-edition.md (cargo fix); Error Prone Refaster and InlineMe docs answered 404 at google/error-prone master docs/refaster.md and docs/bugpattern/InlineMe*.md, so the path must be located before citing
google/eng-practices master review/developer/small-cls.md §'Splitting CLs' and §'Can't Make it Small Enough' — sharding a large change into independently reviewable pieces

SWEBOK V3 community transcription ligurio/swebok-v3: ch. 3 'Software Construction' §3.8 'Integration' and ch. 5 'Software Maintenance' §4 on migration — the README lists no chapter files, so the file path must be located before citing
notes: Owns a change that spans many files, packages or owners and cannot land as one reviewable change: generating the edit with a syntax-aware tool rather than text substitution, sharding it into pieces that each build, pass and can be reverted alone, letting the old and new paths coexist while callers migrate, and finishing the migration by removing the old path and the flag that selected it. Yields the size and shape of one shard to small-steps-and-minimal-diffs; the behaviour preservation of each rewrite to refactoring; deprecation policy and version signalling to api-evolution-and-deprecation; dependency version upgrades to dependency-management; a stale path left behind and recorded to technical-debt. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule that relies on one language's migration tool belongs elsewhere, and the tool may appear in an Example only. SEG22's approval committee and ownership process belong to process and team management, and online data or schema migrations across services belong to distributed systems; both are outside the corpus, as is cross-platform migration.

title: Small steps and minimal diffs
locators: TF (Tidy First? A Personal Exercise in Empirical Software Design, Beck 2023: Part I 'Tidyings'; Part II 'Managing' — 'Separate Tidying', 'Batch Sizes', 'Getting Untangled'; Part III 'Theory' — 'Structure and Behavior'); the openable formulation of the same practice is google/eng-practices 'Small CLs'
candidate_evidence: Herzig, Zeller, 'The impact of tangled code changes' (MSR 2013) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'In an investigation of five open-source Java projects, they found up to 15% of all bug fixes to consist of multiple tangled changes'; 'on average at least 16.6% of all source files are incorrectly associated with bug reports'; 'The authors recommend better change organization to limit the impact of tangled changes' — https://www.st.cs.uni-saarland.de/publications/files/herzig-msr-2013.pdf (author copy)

Barnett, Bird, Brunet, Lahiri, 'Helping developers help themselves: automatic decomposition of code review changesets' (ICSE 2015) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'Understanding a code review is more difficult when the changeset consists of multiple, independent code differences'; 'over 40% of changes submitted for review at Microsoft can be potentially decomposed into multiple partitions' — https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/helping-developers-help-themselves-automatic-decomposition-of-code-review-changesets/

Di Biase, Bruntink, van Deursen, Bacchelli, 'The effects of change decomposition on code review — a controlled experiment' (PeerJ Computer Science 5:e193, 2019; DOI 10.7717/peerj-cs.193; arXiv:1805.10978) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'a controlled experiment with the pull-based development model involving 28 software developers among professionals and graduate students'; 'Change decomposition leads to fewer wrongly reported issues, influences how subjects approach and conduct the review activity (by increasing context-seeking), yet impacts neither understanding the change rationale nor the number of found defects' — https://arxiv.org/pdf/1805.10978; https://peerj.com/articles/cs-193/

Kamei, Shihab, Adams, Hassan, Mockus, Sinha, Ubayashi, 'A large-scale empirical study of just-in-time quality assurance' (IEEE TSE 39(6), 2013, pp. 757–773) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'identifying defect-prone (risky) software changes instead of files or packages'; 'six open source and five commercial projects'; 'predict whether or not a change will lead to a defect with an average accuracy of 68 percent and an average recall of 64 percent'; 'using only 20 percent of the effort it would take to inspect all changes, they can identify 35 percent of all defect-inducing changes' — https://sail.cs.queensu.ca/data/pdfs/TSE_ALarge-ScaleEmpiricalStudyOfJust-in-TimeQualityAssurance.pdf (author copy); the size factors of the model are in the paper, not the snippet

Sadowski, Söderberg, Church, Sipko, Bacchelli, 'Modern code review: a case study at Google' (ICSE SEIP 2018) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: '12 interviews, a survey with 44 respondents, and the analysis of review logs for 9 million reviewed changes' — https://research.google/pubs/pub47025; the change-size figures (median lines changed) are in the paper, not the snippet

official documentation: google/eng-practices master review/developer/small-cls.md (§'Why Write Small CLs?', 'What is Small?', 'Separate Out Refactorings', 'Keep related test code in the same CL', 'Don't Break the Build', 'Splitting CLs')
git/git master Documentation/git-add.adoc (interactive and patch staging, the mechanism for splitting a working tree into one-concern commits)
Tidy First? is a trade book with no openable text — formulation only
notes: Owns the size and shape of one change: one concern per change with no tangled edits, structural tidying and behavioural change in separate commits, a minimal diff without drive-by reformatting, renames or unrelated fixes, tests in the same change as the code they cover, every change building and passing on its own, and splitting large work by stacking or by horizontal and vertical slices. Yields the change description and the reviewer's reading to code-review-as-author-and-reviewer; a migration that spans many owners and shards to large-scale-changes-and-migrations; the safety of each transformation to refactoring. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust and across version-control systems; a rule tied to one tool's workflow belongs elsewhere. Review turnaround targets, team batch policies and release cadence are process and team management and stay outside the corpus.

title: Technical debt
locators: PP 'Software Entropy' (The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th anniversary ed., ch. 1 'A Pragmatic Philosophy', topic 'Software Entropy': broken windows); the 97 Things essays 'Act with Prudence' (en/thing_01/README.md), 'The Boy Scout Rule' (en/thing_08/README.md) and 'The Road to Performance Is Littered with Dirty Code Bombs' (en/thing_74/README.md) in 97-things/97-things-every-programmer-should-know
candidate_evidence: Potdar, Shihab, 'An exploratory study on self-admitted technical debt' (ICSME 2014) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'Eclipse, Chromium OS, Apache HTTP Server, and ArgoUML using source-code comments'; 'Self-admitted technical debt exists in 2.4% -- 31% of the files in the studied projects'; 'Developers with higher experience tend to introduce most of the self-admitted technical debt, and time pressures and complexity of the code do not correlate with the amount of self-admitted technical debt'; 'Only between 26.3% -- 63.5% of self-admitted technical debt gets removed from projects after introduction' — result list: computer.org proceedings entry; a later survey arXiv:2312.15020

Wehaibi, Shihab, Guerrouj, 'Examining the impact of self-admitted technical debt on software quality' (SANER 2016, pp. 179–188) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'whether files with self-admitted technical debt have more defects compared to files without self-admitted technical debt, whether self-admitted technical debt changes introduce future defects, and whether such changes tend to be more difficult'; 'five open source projects: Hadoop, Chromium, Cassandra, Spark and Tomcat' — https://faculty.ksu.edu.sa/sites/default/files/examining_the_impact_of_self-admitted_technical_debt_on_software_quality.pdf (author copy); the findings themselves are in the paper, not the snippet

Bavota, Russo, 'A large-scale empirical study on self-admitted technical debt' (MSR 2016) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'a differentiated replication of work by Potdar and Shihab, running across 159 software projects'; 'mining over 600K commits and 2 Billion comments'; 'an average of 51 self-admitted technical debt comments per system, with SATD consisting of 30% code debt, 20% defect debt, and 20% requirement debt, with SATD comments increasing over time and taking over 1,000 commits on average before being fixed' — https://bia.unibz.it/esploro/outputs/conferenceProceeding/A-Large-Scale-Empirical-Study-on-Self-Admitted/991006853897901241

Levén, Broman, Besker, Torkar, 'The broken windows theory applies to technical debt' (Empirical Software Engineering 29, 2024; DOI 10.1007/s10664-024-10456-6; arXiv:2209.01549) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'a controlled experiment with an accompanying survey and follow-up interviews, involving 29 developers of varying experience levels completing system extension tasks in systems with high or low technical debt density'; 'significant effects of technical debt level on developers' tendency to re-implement rather than reuse functionality, choose non-descriptive variable names, and introduce other code smells, all with at least 95% credible intervals' — https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.01549
Tufano, Palomba, Bavota, Oliveto, Di Penta, De Lucia, Poshyvanyk, 'When and why your code starts to smell bad' (ICSE 2015) — 80% of smells survive; only 9% of removals come from refactoring
Ramanathan, Clapp, Barik, Sridharan, 'Piranha: reducing feature flag debt at Uber' (ICSE SEIP 2020) — stale flags as debt and their automated removal

tool rules on debt markers: ESLint no-warning-comments (eslint/eslint main docs/src/rules/no-warning-comments.md), Pylint fixme (pylint-dev/pylint main pylint/checkers/misc.py), Checkstyle TodoComment (checkstyle/checkstyle master src/site/xdoc/checks/misc/todocomment.xml), Ruff flake8-todos TD rules incl. TD003 missing issue link (crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/flake8_todos/rules/todos.rs) and flake8-fixme FIX rules (flake8_fixme/rules/todos.rs), clippy todo and unimplemented (rust-lang/rust-clippy master clippy_lints/src/panic_unimplemented.rs), SonarSource S1135 'track uses of TODO tags' (sonar-python python-checks/.../python/S1135.html answers 200; the sonar-java path from the source map answers 404 and is not openable as mapped)
notes: Owns the debt a change knowingly takes on or leaves behind: a shortcut or workaround recorded where it lives with an owner and a tracking reference (the todo_marker signal), no new debt added next to known debt (broken windows), the debt a change touches paid down or recorded rather than widened, and stale temporary code such as a rolled-out feature flag's dead branch removed. Yields the individual smells to code-smells-and-antipatterns; the paying-down transformation to refactoring; the comment's wording to comments-and-self-documenting-code; a multi-owner cleanup to large-scale-changes-and-migrations; how configuration and flags are read to runtime-configuration. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a marker convention is 'the project's debt marker', never one linter's spelling. Prioritizing a debt backlog, allocating team capacity to it and estimating its interest are process and team management and estimation, outside the corpus.

title: Debugging
locators: CC23 (Code Complete 2nd ed. ch. 23 'Debugging': finding a defect by the scientific method, fixing a defect, psychological considerations, debugging tools); PoP5 (The Practice of Programming ch. 5 'Debugging': good clues and easy bugs, no clues and hard bugs, non-reproducible bugs, debugging tools); PP 'Debugging' (The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th anniversary ed., ch. 3 'The Basic Tools', topic 'Debugging')
candidate_evidence: Zeller, 'Yesterday, my program worked. Today, it does not. Why?' (ESEC/FSE 1999; LNCS 1687; ACM SIGSOFT Impact Paper Award) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'given a program and a number of changes where none applied means the program works (yesterday) but all applied means it doesn't work (today), which change is responsible for the failure? ... an efficient algorithm that determines the minimal set of failure-inducing changes'; 'The delta debugging prototype tracked down a single failure-inducing change from 178,000 changed GDB lines within a few hours' — https://www.st.cs.uni-saarland.de/publications/files/zeller-esec-1999.pdf (author copy)

Zeller, Hildebrandt, 'Simplifying and isolating failure-inducing input' (IEEE TSE 28(2), 2002, pp. 183–200) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'The Delta Debugging algorithm generalizes and simplifies some failing test case to a minimal test case that still produces the failure; it also isolates the difference between a passing and a failing test case'; 'the Mozilla web browser crashed after 95 user actions. The prototype implementation automatically simplified the input to 3 relevant user actions. Likewise, it simplified 896 lines of HTML to the single line that caused the failure. The case study required 139 automated test runs, or 35 minutes on a 500MHz PC' — https://www.st.cs.uni-saarland.de/papers/tse2002/tse2002.pdf (author copy)

Parnin, Orso, 'Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers?' (ISSTA 2011; ISSTA 2021 Impact Paper Award) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'investigated through two user studies how developers used and benefited from popular automated debugging techniques, and the results provided evidence that several assumptions made by automated debugging techniques did not hold in practice'; 'the assumption that examining a faulty statement in isolation is enough for a developer to understand and fix the corresponding bug' — https://web.eecs.umich.edu/~weimerw/2018-481/readings/debugging-helping.pdf (course copy); the 'experienced developers on easy tasks' finding is in the paper, not the snippet

Beller, Spruit, Spinellis, Zaidman, 'On the dichotomy of debugging behavior among programmers' (ICSE 2018) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'instrumented the popular Eclipse and IntelliJ IDEs with a purpose-built plugin called WatchDog 2.0 to observe how 458 developers use the debugger ... and conducted an online survey capturing how 176 developers reflect on debugging'; 'IDE-provided debuggers are not used as often as expected, because printf debugging remains a feasible choice for many programmers, and both knowledge and use of advanced debugging features are low' — https://www.spinellis.gr/pubs/conf/2018-ICSE-debugging-analysis/html/BSSZ18.pdf (author copy)

Böhme, Soremekun, Chattopadhyay, Ugherughe, Zeller, 'Where is the bug and how is it fixed? An experiment with practitioners' (ESEC/FSE 2017) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'a dataset named DBGBENCH containing the correct fault locations, bug diagnoses, and software patches of 27 real errors in open-source C projects that were consolidated from hundreds of debugging sessions of professional software engineers'; 'how debugging time, difficulty, and strategies vary across practitioners and types of errors' — https://publications.cispa.saarland/1468/1/FSE17.pdf (author copy)

Alaboudi, LaToza, 'Using hypotheses as a debugging aid' (VL/HCC 2020; arXiv:2005.13652) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'a controlled experiment where 20 developers debugged and recorded their hypotheses'; 'incorrect hypotheses can cause developers to investigate irrelevant information and block progress'; 'Developers typically have few hypotheses — two per defect — and having a correct hypothesis early strongly predicted later success'; 'Offering fault locations did not help developers formulate more correct hypotheses or debug more successfully, but offering potential hypotheses made developers six times more likely to succeed' — https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.13652

Alaboudi, LaToza, 'What constitutes debugging? An exploratory study of debugging episodes' (Empirical Software Engineering 28, 2023; DOI 10.1007/s10664-023-10352-5; arXiv:2105.02162) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'a debugging episode ... the time from when a developer first investigates a defect until when the defect is fixed or the developer stops'; '15 sessions in which 11 professional developers worked for 30 hours'; '89 distinct debugging episodes spanning more than 15 hours of debugging time as well as 13 hours of programming time'; 'six activities that occurred during debugging episodes across 2135 instances' — https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.02162

tool rules on debugging aids left in code: ESLint no-debugger and no-console (eslint/eslint main docs/src/rules/no-debugger.md, no-console.md), Ruff flake8-debugger T100 (crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/flake8_debugger/rules/debugger.rs) and flake8-print T201/T203 (flake8_print/rules/print_call.rs), clippy dbg_macro (rust-lang/rust-clippy master clippy_lints/src/dbg_macro.rs)

official documentation: git/git master Documentation/git-bisect.adoc (the .txt path answers 404); python/cpython main Doc/library/pdb.rst; rust-lang/rust master library/std/src/macros.rs (the dbg! macro's documentation)
notes: Owns finding and fixing a defect: reproduce the failure first and capture it as a failing test, narrow it by explicit hypotheses and experiments rather than by random edits, shrink the failing input or bisect the history when the cause is not evident, fix the cause rather than the symptom and look for the same defect elsewhere, keep the reproducing test as a regression test, and remove temporary debugging aids (debugger statements, stray prints) before the change lands. Yields permanent diagnostic output and log levels to logging-and-diagnostic-output; the regression test's structure and assertions to unit-testing-and-test-quality; slowness as the symptom to profiling-and-code-tuning; the local handling of a failure to error-and-exception-handling; reading unfamiliar code to reading-and-understanding-code. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a debugger or a language's print facility may appear in an Example only. Data races, deadlocks and other concurrency failures belong to the reserved concurrency-correctness specialty, and tracing across services belongs to distributed systems; both are outside the corpus, and the agent names them and stops.

title: Profiling and code tuning
locators: CC25 (Code Complete 2nd ed. ch. 25 'Code-Tuning Strategies'); CC26 (Code Complete 2nd ed. ch. 26 'Code-Tuning Techniques'); PoP7 (The Practice of Programming ch. 7 'Performance': a bottleneck, timing and profiling, strategies for speed, tuning the code, space efficiency, estimation); SW4.14 (SWEBOK Guide V4.0 ch. 4 'Software Construction' §4.14)
candidate_evidence: Mytkowicz, Diwan, Hauswirth, Sweeney, 'Evaluating the accuracy of Java profilers' (PLDI 2010, pp. 187–197; DOI 10.1145/1806596.1806618) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'four commonly-used Java profilers (xprof, hprof, jprofile, and yourkit) often disagree on the identity of the hot methods'; 'these profilers all violate a fundamental requirement for sampling-based profilers: to be correct, a sampling-based profiler must collect samples randomly' — https://plv.colorado.edu/papers/profilers-pldi10.html (author page)

Burchell, Larose, Kaleba, Marr, 'Don't trust your profiler: an empirical study on the precision and accuracy of Java profilers' (MPLR 2023; DOI 10.1145/3617651.3622985) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'evaluates the precision, reliability, accuracy, and overhead of async-profiler, Honest Profiler, Java Flight Recorder, JProfiler, perf, and YourKit'; 'Profilers are relatively reliable over 30 runs and normally report the same hottest method, though this is not true for all benchmarks'; 'Different profilers report different methods as hottest and cannot reliably agree on the set of top 5 hottest methods'; 'The average run time overhead is in the range of 1% to 5.4%' — https://stefan-marr.de/downloads/mplr23-burchell-et-al-dont-trust-your-profiler.pdf (author copy)

Mytkowicz, Diwan, Hauswirth, Sweeney, 'Producing wrong data without doing anything obviously wrong!' (ASPLOS 2009) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'changing a seemingly innocuous aspect of an experimental setup can cause a systems researcher to draw wrong conclusions from an experiment'; 'measurement bias is significant and commonplace in computer system evaluation'; 'Measurement bias occurs in all architectures that were tried (Pentium 4, Core 2, and m5 O3CPU), both compilers that were tried (gcc and Intel's C compiler), and most of the SPEC CPU2006 C programs'; 'In a literature survey of 133 recent papers from ASPLOS, PACT, PLDI, and CGO, none of the papers with experimental results adequately considered measurement bias'; remedies 'causal analysis' and 'setup randomization' — https://sape.inf.usi.ch/publications/asplos09 (author page)

Georges, Buytaert, Eeckhout, 'Statistically rigorous Java performance evaluation' (OOPSLA 2007) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'non-determinism at run-time that causes execution time to differ from run to run, stemming from sources like Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation and optimization in the virtual machine driven by timer-based method sampling, thread scheduling, garbage collection, and various system effects' — https://dri.es/files/oopsla07-georges.pdf (author copy); the confidence-interval methodology is in the paper, not the snippet

Curtsinger, Berger, 'Coz: finding code that counts with causal profiling' (SOSP 2015, best paper; arXiv:1608.03676) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'causal profiling, which indicates exactly where programmers should focus their optimization efforts and quantifies their potential impact'; 'calculating the impact of potential optimizations by virtually speeding up code through inserting pauses that slow down all other concurrent code'; 'improved Memcached's performance by 9%, SQLite by 25%, and accelerated six PARSEC applications by as much as 68%' — the tool and paper link at github.com/plasma-umass/coz (README openable through raw.githubusercontent.com); https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/~ey204/teaching/ACS/R212_2015_2016/papers/curtsinger_SOSP_2015.pdf (course copy)

Jin, Song, Shi, Scherpelz, Lu, 'Understanding and detecting real-world performance bugs' (PLDI 2012) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: '109 real-world performance bugs randomly sampled from five representative software suites: Apache, Chrome, GCC, Mozilla, and MySQL'; 'Efficiency rules were extracted from 25 patches and used to detect performance bugs, finding 332 previously unknown performance problems in the latest versions of MySQL, Apache, and Mozilla applications, including 219 performance problems found by applying rules across applications' — https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~songlh/perf-detect.html (author page); https://ece.uwaterloo.ca/~wshang/soen691/current/papers/pldi118-jin.pdf (course copy)

Nistor, Jiang, Tan, 'Discovering, reporting, and fixing performance bugs' (MSR 2013) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'bugs from three popular code bases: Eclipse JDT, Eclipse SWT, and Mozilla'; 'Little evidence was found that fixing performance bugs has a higher chance to introduce new functional bugs'; 'fixing performance bugs is more difficult than fixing non-performance bugs'; 'a large percentage of performance bugs are discovered through code reasoning, not through users observing negative effects or through profiling' — https://www.cs.purdue.edu/homes/lintan/publications/perf-msr13-preprint.pdf (author preprint)

official documentation of profilers and benchmark harnesses: python/cpython main Doc/library/profile.rst, timeit.rst, tracemalloc.rst; golang/go master src/testing/testing.go §'Benchmarks' and src/runtime/pprof/pprof.go; golang/website master _content/doc/diagnostics.html; openjdk/jmh master README.md; bheisler/criterion.rs master README.md; SWEBOK V3 ch. 3 §4.14 'Performance Analysis and Tuning' in ligurio/swebok-v3, file path to locate

tool rules on ordinary inefficiencies: PMD performance category (pmd/pmd main pmd-java/src/main/resources/category/java/performance.xml: InefficientStringBuffering, UseStringBufferForStringAppends, AvoidInstantiatingObjectsInLoops), Ruff perflint PERF rules (crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/perflint/rules/try_except_in_loop.rs, unnecessary_list_cast.rs, incorrect_dict_iterator.rs, manual_list_comprehension.rs), SpotBugs PERFORMANCE category (spotbugs/spotbugs master spotbugs/etc/messages.xml)
notes: Owns measure before tuning: no tuning without a measurement that shows a need, a profile to find where the time goes before choosing what to change, a benchmark that warms up, repeats and reports variation against a baseline, re-measuring after each change and reverting tuning that does not pay, keeping the clear version where the measurement does not justify the tuned one, and recording the measurement with the change. Yields the complexity class and the standard-library structure to algorithm-and-data-structure-choice; leaked or unreleased resources to resource-management-and-ownership; a wrong result found while measuring to debugging; build and compiler settings to build-warnings-static-analysis-ci. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a profiler or benchmark harness may appear in an Example only. Low-latency and high-frequency-trading tuning (cache-line layout, lock-free structures, allocation-free hot paths, runtime and garbage-collector tuning) is a reserved specialty, as is parallelization under concurrency correctness; the rules stop at measure before tuning and the agent names the specialty and stops.

title: Algorithm and data structure choice
locators: PoP2 (The Practice of Programming ch. 2 'Algorithms and Data Structures': searching, sorting, libraries, O-notation, growing arrays, lists, trees, hash tables); PP 'Algorithm Speed' (The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th anniversary ed., ch. 7 'While You Are Coding', topic 'Algorithm Speed')
candidate_evidence: Shacham, Vechev, Yahav, 'Chameleon: adaptive selection of collections' (PLDI 2009, pp. 408–418) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: title, venue and pages confirmed; no abstract text in the results, so the paper is unfetched unless a GitHub-hosted copy is found — cited by arXiv:1706.03232 (Darwinian data structure selection)

Costa, Andrzejak, Seboek, Lo, 'Empirical study of usage and performance of Java collections' (ICPE 2017) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'Collection data structures have a major impact on the performance of applications, especially in languages such as Java, C#, or C++ ... there exist a large variety of less known third-party collection libraries which can provide substantial performance benefits with minimal code changes' — https://research.spec.org/icpe_proceedings/2017/proceedings/p389.pdf (open proceedings PDF); the benchmark at github.com/DiegoEliasCosta/CollectionsBench (README openable through raw.githubusercontent.com); the 10,986-project and 60–88% figures are in the paper, not the snippet

Basios, Li, Wu, Kanthan, Barr, 'Darwinian data structure selection' (ESEC/FSE 2018; arXiv:1706.03232) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'Darwinian Data Structures (DDS) where multiple implementations of data structures with a common interface can compete'; 'ARTEMIS ... evaluated on 43 Java projects, finding at least one solution that improves all measures (execution time, CPU usage, and memory consumption) for 86% of them, with median improvements of 4.8%, 10.1%, and 5.1% for runtime, memory, and CPU usage respectively' — https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03232

Olivo, Dillig, Lin, 'Static detection of asymptotic performance bugs in collection traversals' (PLDI 2015) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: 'a prevalent class of asymptotic performance bugs called redundant traversal bugs'; 'the tool CLARITY ... applied it to widely-used software packages such as the Google Core Collections Library, the Apache Common Collections, and the Apache Ant build tool. Across 1.6M lines of Java code, CLARITY finds 92 instances of redundant traversal bugs, including 72 that have never been previously reported, with just 5 false positives'; 'For an input size of 50,000, all repaired programs are at least 2.45× faster than their original code' — https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~lin/papers/pldi15.pdf (author copy)

Selakovic, Pradel, 'Performance issues and optimizations in JavaScript: an empirical study' (ICSE 2016; DOI 10.1145/2884781.2884829) — relayed by the orchestrator's search: '98 fixed performance issues from 16 popular client-side and server-side JavaScript projects'; 'Eight root causes of issues were identified, with inefficient usage of APIs being the most prevalent root cause'; 'Most issues were addressed by optimizations that modified only a few lines of code'; 'only 42.68% of all optimizations improved performance consistently across all versions of both engines' — https://tuprints.ulb.tu-darmstadt.de/server/api/core/bitstreams/ad7a897e-da4f-41ba-8d89-c4772f9c23f2/content (institutional copy)
Jin, Song, Shi, Scherpelz, Lu, 'Understanding and detecting real-world performance bugs' (PLDI 2012)

official documentation of collection costs: rust-lang/rust master library/std/src/collections/mod.rs ('When Should You Use Which Collection?', 'Cost of Collection Operations'); openjdk/jdk jdk-21-ga src/java.base/share/classes/java/util/ArrayList.java and LinkedList.java class documentation on operation cost; python/cpython main Doc/library/collections.rst (deque), bisect.rst, heapq.rst; golang/go master src/container/heap/heap.go; tc39/ecma262 main spec.html (Map and Set must provide access times sublinear in the number of elements)

tool rules: clippy linkedlist (rust-lang/rust-clippy master clippy_lints/src/types/mod.rs, LINKEDLIST), Ruff PLR6201 literal-membership (crates/ruff_linter/src/rules/pylint/rules/literal_membership.rs), PMD performance UseArrayListInsteadOfVector (category/java/performance.xml); SonarSource S2250 on collection methods with O(n) performance — the sonar-java path from the source map answers 404 and is not openable as mapped
notes: Owns the complexity class of the chosen structure for the observed size and the ordinary standard-library choice: a hashed set or map for repeated membership tests or lookups by key instead of a scan inside a loop, a deque or an index instead of repeated removal from the front of an array, one indexing pass instead of a nested traversal of two collections, the library's sort, binary search and heap instead of a hand-rolled one, and linear accumulation instead of quadratic string or array building in a loop. Yields measuring whether the choice matters to profiling-and-code-tuning; the type that models a domain value to domain-modeling-and-domain-language; shared mutable collections to mutable-state-and-immutability. Rules must hold across Java, Python, TypeScript, Go and Rust; a rule names the operation and its cost class, and one language's collection type appears in an Example only. Algorithm research (novel algorithms, proofs of bounds, probabilistic or cache-oblivious structures) and low-latency tuning are reserved specialties, and algorithmic-complexity denial of service belongs to security-critical design; the rules stop at the complexity class for the observed size and the standard-library choice.
